name: The magistrates of Philippi
charge: Beating and imprisoning uncondemned Romans on the word of a mob
summary: A damsel possessed with a spirit of divination brought her masters much gain by soothsaying and followed the apostles through the streets, until Paul turned and commanded the spirit to come out of her. When her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone they drew Paul and Silas into the marketplace to the rulers, and the multitude rose up together against them. The magistrates rent off their clothes and commanded to beat them, laid many stripes upon them, and cast them into prison, with no trial and no condemnation. In the morning they sent to let them go privily, and Paul refused.
offenseFull: As they went to the place where prayer was made, a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met them, who brought her masters much gain by soothsaying; she was a kind of fortune teller, and she followed Paul and the others through the streets crying out that these men are the servants of the most high God, which show us the way of salvation, and she did this many days (Acts 16:16-17). Even the spirit in her knew who the prophets of God were, when the woman’s own family and friends would not. Paul, patient as he was, was grieved with it at last and turned and commanded the spirit to come out of her, and it came out the same hour (Acts 16:18). That is no different from today, when men come up at camp talking nonsense with a cross in their hand, and brothers have to be set aside to deal with the spirit before it gets to the people.

When her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone they caught Paul and Silas and drew them into the marketplace to the rulers, and brought them to the magistrates, saying that these men, being Jews, did exceedingly trouble their city and taught customs which were not lawful for them to receive nor to observe, being Romans (Acts 16:19-21). The charge they brought in public was not the loss that had actually moved them; the real complaint was money, and the public complaint was that these Jews were troubling the city. That is coming to the good old USA, and our men should read it as a rehearsal and not as ancient news. The multitude rose up together against them, and the magistrates rent off their clothes and commanded to beat them, and when they had laid many stripes upon them they cast them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely (Acts 16:22-23). There had been no hearing and no sentence, and the law of the Most High requires judges and officers who will not wrest judgment nor respect persons, and limits even a lawful beating (Deuteronomy 16:18-19, Deuteronomy 25:1-3).
judgmentFull: When it was day the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying to let those men go, and the keeper told Paul that he might depart in peace; but Paul said that they had beaten them openly, uncondemned, being Romans, and had cast them into prison, and now would thrust them out privily, and that the magistrates must come themselves and fetch them out (Acts 16:35-37). You gave us a public beating and threw us into prison in public, and now you want to release us quietly through your errand men. It does not work that way. Roman citizenship guaranteed a man some degree of protection of his person and his goods, and that protection is what Paul invoked here and again at Jerusalem, where he asked the centurion whether it was lawful to scourge a man that is a Roman and uncondemned, and the chief captain was afraid when he learned it (Acts 22:25-29). That citizenship functioned as his papers, the way a passport works today, and the men who had bound him had to take a step back the moment it was produced.

The serjeants told these words to the magistrates, and they feared when they heard that they were Romans, and came and besought them, and brought them out, and desired them to depart out of the city (Acts 16:38-39). The record gives that reversal and no further penalty upon the magistrates. Paul and Silas then went to Lydia’s house, comforted the brethren, and departed (Acts 16:40). The authorities who had treated them as criminals in the morning had to walk to the prison themselves in the evening. Paul counted that day as shameful treatment and wrote of it afterward, saying that even after they had suffered and were shamefully entreated at Philippi they were bold in their God to speak the gospel with much contention (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

text.text: And it came to pass, as we went to prayer, a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met us, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying:
The same followed Paul and us, and cried, saying, These men are the servants of the most high God, which shew unto us the way of salvation.
And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour.
And when her masters saw that the hope of their gains was gone, they caught Paul and Silas, and drew them into the marketplace unto the rulers,
And brought them to the magistrates, saying, These men, being Jews, do exceedingly trouble our city,
And teach customs, which are not lawful for us to receive, neither to observe, being Romans.
And the multitude rose up together against them: and the magistrates rent off their clothes, and commanded to beat them.
And when they had laid many stripes upon them, they cast them into prison, charging the jailor to keep them safely:
Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the Lord thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment, that the judges may judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked.
And it shall be, if the wicked man be worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his fault, by a certain number.
Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.
And when it was day, the magistrates sent the serjeants, saying, Let those men go.
And the keeper of the prison told this saying to Paul, The magistrates have sent to let you go: now therefore depart, and go in peace.

But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?
When the centurion heard that, he went and told the chief captain, saying, Take heed what thou doest: for this man is a Roman.
Then the chief captain came, and said unto him, Tell me, art thou a Roman? He said, Yea.
And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born.
Then straightway they departed from him which should have examined him: and the chief captain also was afraid, after he knew that he was a Roman, and because he had bound him.
And the serjeants told these words unto the magistrates: and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans.
And they came and besought them, and brought them out, and desired them to depart out of the city.
And they went out of the prison, and entered into the house of Lydia: and when they had seen the brethren, they comforted them, and departed.
But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention.
